title: Authentication and Session Lifecycle
readerIntent: Understand login, tokens, browser restoration, revocation, and internal credentials.
owner: Profile login/session services and nAuth credential contracts
summary: Human login issues human tokens; service identity issues internal tokens; refresh rotation and security stamps invalidate sessions without storing usable credentials in clients, logs, or audit.

sections.heading: Human authentication
items: Employee and customer username/password routes are pre-authentication routes but still resolve enterprise and tenant context.
Access tokens are short-lived and audience-bound; target authorization always follows.
Browser restoration keeps refresh credentials in scoped HttpOnly cookies, requires exact Origin and CSRF proof, atomically consumes refresh state, and rotates credentials.
Logout revokes refresh state and expires cookies; lock screen does not silently weaken server session policy.

sections.heading: Internal authentication
items: Service principals own API keys stored as keyed digests.
Internal service tokens are tenant-aware, permissioned, bounded, and issued through the service-token contract.
Service-only routes declare authTokenTypes and reject human tokens even when permissions overlap.
Cron and controlled scheduled work use service identity, not employee credentials.

sections.heading: Employee session example
items: An Axis employee submits username and password only to the configured Profile employee-authentication route with the required tenant and enterprise context. Customer authentication is a separate route and cannot open Axis.

On success the backend issues a short-lived access token for API calls and, where configured, a rotating refresh credential in a Secure, HttpOnly, narrowly scoped cookie. JavaScript does not persist refresh secrets.

A browser refresh restores the session through the refresh contract only after exact Origin, CSRF, tenant, device/session, expiry, revocation, and security-stamp checks. Rotation atomically invalidates the previous refresh state.

Axis lock mode hides the workspace and requires re-entry according to policy, but it does not extend token lifetime or replace server-side revocation. Logout consumes refresh state and expires the cookie.

sections.heading: Module and scheduled-process example
items: A CMS process that registers with BackOffice authenticates as its own service principal after startup. Registration is asynchronous and resilient, but the credential remains bounded to the declared audience, tenant, permissions, and lifetime.
A scheduled job obtains service identity through the same internal contract appropriate to cron execution. It never stores or replays an administrator's password or employee bearer token.

The receiving module declares accepted token classes and independently authorizes the requested operation. A valid employee token cannot enter a service-only route, and a service token cannot impersonate a human workflow decision.

Keys are stored as digests with a governed pepper, rotated under audit, and never returned after creation. Token issuance, caching, revocation, and stamp changes must behave consistently across all running nodes.

sections.heading: Failure and proof
items: Fail closed on missing secrets, tenant context, distributed atomic refresh state, stamp state, scope, or permission.
Test wrong credentials, inactive/locked principals, replay, concurrent refresh, expiry, revocation, stamp changes, cross-tenant use, service-only rejection, and distributed invalidation.

sections.heading: Operational troubleshooting
items: A 401 indicates authentication could not establish an acceptable principal; a 403 indicates an established principal lacks authority. Public responses stay generic while protected diagnostics use correlation identifiers.

When all logins fail, verify the intended environment, tenant, bootstrap or imported identities, credential migration state, JWT secrets, API-key pepper, clocks, shared refresh/revocation store, proxy TLS, cookie scope, Origin, and CSRF configuration.
Fail closed when distributed atomic refresh state is required but unavailable. Local fallback that permits replay on another node is not an availability improvement.

Monitor outcome categories, latency, lockouts, replay, refresh rotation, revocation, stamp mismatch, service-token issuance, and cache health using bounded labels that do not expose identifiers or secrets.
